description: Two computer engineering students from Ankara tackling the Lunar Landing Site Navigator (CLPS) challenge. We’re building a tool that compares Moon south pole landing sites and dates by computing Sun and Earth visibility over real LOLA terrain horizons: power and comms windows at a glance. We cover ephemeris, terrain processing and the web app.
summary:
LineOfSight is a browser-based Lunar Landing Site Navigator for the Moon's south pole. A mission planner picks two complete landing plans (site + date + hour) and within seconds sees which one keeps the lander in sunlight for power and in line of sight to Earth for direct radio.

At the pole the Sun circles along the horizon and Earth bobs up and down with libration, so a few hundred metres or a few days decide whether a lander has power and a radio link. Today's tools (JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, QuickMap) are built for experts and need ephemeris and terrain to be combined by hand.

LineOfSight computes a 360° skyline from NASA LRO LOLA terrain for 17 curated sites (CLPS, Artemis study regions, Apollo, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e) or any custom south-pole point, and combines it with Sun and Earth positions that match NASA/JPL Horizons within 0.003°. It outputs a one-sentence verdict, a 30-day comparison table, an hour-by-hour timeline, a pad-level grid with NASA PGDA slope and permanent-shadow checks, CSV export and a shareable link. It is a static web app: no install, no server, $0 to run. Results are screening estimates, not certified pad assessments.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

LineOfSight compares two complete landing plans (site + date + hour) in four steps:

1. Pick: choose a site on a shaded LOLA map of the south pole, or click any point on the terrain. 17 curated sites are included (NASA south-pole study regions, CLPS landings IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost 1, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, Chang'e 4/6, Apollo 11/14).

2. Compare: a one-sentence verdict and a 30-day table (time in sunlight, time Earth is in view, both together, longest darkness, longest radio gap, mean Sun height, pad slope), plus an hour-by-hour timeline.

3. Inspect: a 360° skyline panorama from the lander with the Sun's and Earth's 30-day paths, and live readouts such as "Sunset in 11 d 5 h".

4. Refine and share: a 5x5 grid of pads 1 km apart coloured by sunlight and Earth view, steep (>10°) or permanently shadowed pads flagged, a Landing safety panel, CSV export, and a link that stores the whole comparison.

HOW IT WORKS

- Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA polar DEMs (80 m/px near the pad, 240 m/px out to the far horizon).

- Skyline: for an observer 2 m above the pad, the highest terrain angle in each of 720 directions (0.5° steps) out to 450 km, including lunar curvature. There is no atmosphere, so no refraction is applied.

- Sun and Earth: topocentric azimuth/elevation from astronomy-engine (VSOP87, ELP, IAU lunar orientation including libration). The same math runs in Python and in the browser.

- Visibility: a body counts as visible when the centre of its disc is above the skyline at its azimuth.

- Safety: NASA GSFC PGDA slope maps (80 m/px and 5 m/px, with 1σ) and the permanent-shadow map (20 m/px).

VALIDATION

- Sun and Earth positions vs NASA/JPL Horizons (3 sites): max difference 0.003°, about 1/170 of the Sun's 0.53° disc. An independent re-run on 13 samples gave 0.0032°.

- Terrain georeferencing at the IM-1 Odysseus touchdown point: our DEM gives 2594 m and a 10.9° slope; PGDA gives 11.2° ± 0.2°; reported values are 2579 m (LROC) and ~12°.

- Browser skylines for custom points (480 m grid) vs the 80 m pipeline: within 0.6° rms at the curated sites.

WHAT IT REVEALS

The best place for power is not the best place for radio. For 2027, Connecting Ridge sees the Sun 88% of the year but Earth only 51%, while Malapert Massif and Leibnitz Beta see Earth 80%+ of the time with much less sun. No polar site gets both, so every plan needs either batteries for a long night or a relay for a long radio gap. The date matters (for a 1 Dec 2026 landing, Connecting Ridge has 100% sunlight but a 12.8 d radio gap, Malapert 78% and 5.1 d) and so does 1 km of pad position (0% to 100% sunlight over 30 days).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Mission planners (CLPS, Artemis, other agencies) can screen site/date trade-offs in seconds, with slope, permanent shadow, uncertainty and CSV export.

- Educators and students get an interactive explanation of why polar landings are so sensitive to place and time.

- The general public gets a plain-language verdict and colours: gold = Sun, blue = Earth.

CREATIVITY

It compares plans (site + date + hour), not just sites, and writes the verdict in one sentence instead of showing raw ephemeris tables. NASA slope and shadow maps become pad-level checks next to the light and comms answer. Any south-pole point can be evaluated live in the browser, with no server.

HONEST LIMITS

- Pad placement: some NASA region centres sit on crater walls, so the tool moves the pad to the highest cell within 1.5 km with slope < 8°. This makes results optimistic by design, and the UI shows the offset.

- Visibility is a clear geometric line of sight, not a power or link budget (no panel orientation, thermal behaviour or antenna gain).

- 80 m and 5 m maps cannot see rocks or holes smaller than ~0.5 m; sites beyond 80°S use a smooth-sphere horizon, and the UI says so.

- Every site is a screened candidate, not a certified landing pad.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, SciPy, tifffile, Pillow) for the offline data pipeline; astronomy-engine (MIT); vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS for a static web app hosted on GitHub Pages ($0 running cost, works offline from a clone).

NEXT STEPS

Relay-satellite visibility, a solar-panel power model, sub-metre roughness (LROC NAC DTMs), rock abundance (Diviner), and the lunar north pole.
